Justifier
JUS-tih-fy-ur
n. (one who declares another righteous; a title of God in the gospel)
From Latin justus, righteous, and facere, to make or declare — through Old French justifier. It renders the participle of Greek dikaioo, to pronounce righteous, a courtroom verb rather than a workshop one.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs once, and it is the hinge of Romans. Paul has spent two and a half chapters proving that every mouth is stopped and all the world guilty before God, and the question that follows is not how God can be merciful — anyone can be lenient — but how he can acquit the guilty without ceasing to be just. A judge who lets the wicked go is himself wicked; Proverbs says he that justifieth the wicked is abomination to the LORD. Paul's answer is the propitiation set forth in the blood of Christ, and the conclusion he draws is stated with deliberate care: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. Not just although he justifies, and not merciful instead of just, but both at once, and by the same act. The cross is what makes the sentence lawful. Everything follows from that. God justifieth the ungodly, and the faith of the man who worketh not is counted for righteousness — counted, not created. It is God that justifieth, and therefore no charge can be laid against his elect. To call God the Justifier is to say that the verdict over a believing sinner is not a lowering of the standard but a satisfaction of it, obtained elsewhere and credited here.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one who justifies; one who vindicates, defends or absolves; he that pardons and clears from guilt.

expand to see more

JUSTIFIER, n. One who justifies; one who vindicates, supports or defends.

JUSTIFIER, n. He that pardons and absolves from guilt and punishment.

JUSTIFY, v.t. In theology, to pardon and clear from guilt; to absolve or acquit from guilt and merited punishment.

IMPUTE, v.t. To charge; to attribute; to set to the account of; to reckon to one what does not belong to him.

PROPITIATION, n. The atonement or atoning sacrifice offered to God to assuage his wrath and render him propitious to sinners.

Key Scripture

Romans 3:26 — "To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus."

Romans 4:5 — "But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness."

Romans 8:33 — "Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth."

Galatians 2:16 — "Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified."

Modern Corruption

Justification is softened into acceptance — God overlooking sin because he is loving — when Paul's whole labour is to show that God did not overlook it, and that the verdict cost a death.

expand to see more

The popular gospel says God accepts you as you are, and stops. Scripture says something more costly and more permanent. Acceptance without satisfaction would make God unjust, and an unjust God is no refuge for anyone — a judge who winks at one man's crimes will wink at the crimes committed against him. Paul insists that the mercy shewn to the believer was purchased at the price of the Son's blood, so that God is simultaneously the one who upholds the law and the one who acquits the lawbreaker. Remove the propitiation and justifier becomes a synonym for indulgence, and the comfort of Romans 8 evaporates with it: no charge can be laid only because the charge was already answered.

Rome's error runs the other way and is older: to make justification a process by which grace is infused and the sinner gradually made righteous enough to be declared so. The Confession answers that those whom God effectually calleth he also freely justifieth, not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous. The distinction is not academic. If the verdict waits on the process, no man knows where he stands; if the verdict is declared at once on the ground of Christ's obedience received by faith, then being justified by faith we have peace with God — present tense, and not subject to review.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dikaioo (G1344), to declare righteous; dikaiosune (G1343), righteousness; logizomai (G3049), to reckon or impute; hilasterion (G2435), the propitiation.

expand to see more

Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to pronounce righteous; a forensic verb, used of a verdict and never of a repair.

Greek dikaion — just; Paul sets it beside justifier in one clause so that neither may be surrendered.

Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to place to an account; the accounting word of Romans 4.

Greek hilasterion (G2435) — the propitiation, the mercy seat; the ground on which the verdict is lawful.

Greek asebes (G765) — ungodly; the man God is said to justify, which is the offence and the gospel together.

Usage

"“that he might be just, and the justifier” — both held in one clause."

"“him that justifieth the ungodly” — the only sort of man there is to justify."

"“It is God that justifieth” — the answer to every accuser."
